raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: Coal trajectory — share peaked 1910, absolute volume still rising in 2024
raw_evidence.content: Coal's share of global primary energy peaked at 55.22% in 1910 — the high-water mark of the steam-and-railway era. Its share then fell as oil and gas took share, dropping to 22.45% by 2000 before partially recovering to 24.60% by 2024 (Chinese industrial growth being the dominant cause). Crucially, coal's share has fallen but its absolute consumption has not: 1910 = 9,136 TWh; 2024 = 45,851 TWh. Coal hit its absolute volume peak in 2024 — the most recent year in the dataset. Despite a century of cleaner alternatives being available, we burn five times as much coal now as at the supposed apex of the coal age. This is the empirical case for Smil's slow-transition thesis: even after a fuel loses share, displacement of absolute volume happens decades later, if at all.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_03 ===")
coal_share = (df["Coal"] / df["Total"]) * 100
coal_tab = pd.DataFrame({"Year": df.Year, "Coal_TWh": df.Coal.round(1), "Coal_share_pct": coal_share.round(2)})
peak_idx = coal_share.idxmax()
print(f"Coal peak share: {coal_share.iloc[peak_idx]:.2f}% in {int(df.Year.iloc[peak_idx])}")
print(f"Coal absolute peak (TWh): {df.Coal.max():.0f} in {int(df.Year.iloc[df.Coal.idxmax()])}")
for y in [1800, 1850, 1900, 1950, 2000, 2024]:
    row = df[df.Year == y]
    if not row.empty:
        i = row.index[0]

In absolute TWh, fossil consumption has grown from 53,387 TWh (1970) to 142,421 TWh (2024) — nearly 3x more. So although renewables and nuclear have prevented the fossil share from continuing to expand, they have not actually pushed the world's fossil consumption down: every year of the 21st century has seen more fossil burning than the year before, with the partial exception of pandemic-affected 2020.

raw_evidence.label: Coal trajectory — share peaked 1910, absolute volume still rising in 2024
raw_evidence.content: Coal's share of global primary energy peaked at 55.22% in 1910 — the high-water mark of the steam-and-railway era. Its share then fell as oil and gas took share, dropping to 22.45% by 2000 before partially recovering to 24.60% by 2024 (Chinese industrial growth being the dominant cause). Crucially, coal's share has fallen but its absolute consumption has not: 1910 = 9,136 TWh; 2024 = 45,851 TWh. Coal hit its absolute volume peak in 2024 — the most recent year in the dataset. Despite a century of cleaner alternatives being available, we burn five times as much coal now as at the supposed apex of the coal age. This is the empirical case for Smil's slow-transition thesis: even after a fuel loses share, displacement of absolute volume happens decades later, if at all.

raw_evidence.label: Global energy mix 1800-2024 — the spine stacked-area data
raw_evidence.content: The core__global-energy-by-source.csv file gives the world's primary-energy supply by source from 1800 through 2024, in TWh/year on the OWID substitution-method convention. In 1800 the entire global energy supply was 5,653 TWh, of which 5,556 TWh (98.3%) was traditional biomass (wood, dung, peat) and 97 TWh (1.7%) was coal — essentially the energy mix of antiquity, with coal as a thin sliver visible mainly in Britain. By 2024 the total was 186,383 TWh — a 33-fold increase over 224 years — with traditional biomass having shrunk to 11,111 TWh (6.0%) and ten distinct other sources now in play. The transformation is not one revolution but four stacked on top of each other: each new fuel was added without the previous one being retired.

raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: Pre-Watt English coal: already 48x its 1508 level by 1800
raw_evidence.content: The Bank of England industrial-production series shows English coal output (in BoE-indexed units, with 1700 = 100) grew from 8.8 in 1508 to 421.3 in 1800 — a 48x increase over the three centuries before James Watt's separate-condenser steam engine reached commercial scale. By 1700 the index was already at 100 (an 11.4x increase from 1508), entirely pre-Watt. Then 1700-1800 added another 4.2x, bringing the index to 421. The pre-Watt growth was real and large — the steam engine accelerated an existing fuel transition rather than starting one. From 1800 to 1850 the index leapt from 421 to 1,913 — a 4.5x jump in just 50 years that dwarfs the entire 300-year pre-1800 growth. The 19th-century explosion was the Watt-and-railway era; the 16th-18th-century growth was domestic heating, brewing, salt-boiling, and iron-smelting demand that justified building the coastal coal trade out of Newcastle.

print("=== ana_16 ===")
coal = uk[["Year", "Coal"]].dropna().reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"English coal series: {len(coal)} rows, year range {int(coal.Year.min())}-{int(coal.Year.max())}")
print("Snapshots (BoE-indexed units; pre-modern reconstruction):")
def nearest_row(target):
    idx = (coal.Year - target).abs().idxmin()
    return coal.iloc[idx]
for y in [1500, 1600, 1700, 1750, 1800, 1850, 1870]:
    nearest = nearest_row(y)
    print(f"  ~{y}: Coal = {nearest.Coal:.3f}  (actual year shown: {int(nearest.Year)})")

# Growth multipliers — use nearest-available years
v_start = nearest_row(1500).Coal  # may snap forward to first available
v_1700 = nearest_row(1700).Coal

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

sources.title: The Steam Engine in the British Industrial Revolution — World History Encyclopedia

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Fuel onset years — when each source first appears in the global mix
raw_evidence.content: The OWID series records the first year each primary-energy source registers a non-zero global contribution: coal (1800, but actually centuries earlier in England — the file just starts at 1800), oil (1870, 6 TWh), natural gas and hydropower (both 1890, 33 and 39 TWh respectively), nuclear (1965, 71 TWh — eleven years after Obninsk's grid connection), wind (1978, 0.01 TWh, essentially noise from California's first commercial turbines), and solar (1983, 0.01 TWh, from early grid-tied photovoltaic experiments). Modern biofuels and 'other renewables' (geothermal, tide, wave) both register from 1965. The clustering of new sources at 1890 (oil scaling, hydro emerging) and 1965 (nuclear, biofuels, geothermal) matches the textbook periodisation of the 2nd and 3rd industrial revolutions almost exactly.
raw_evidence.code:
onset = []
for col in FUEL_COLS:
    nonzero = df.loc[df[col] > 0, "Year"]
    yr = int(nonzero.iloc[0]) if len(nonzero) else None
    val0 = df.loc[df[col] > 0, col].iloc[0] if len(nonzero) else None
    onset.append((col, yr, val0))
onset.sort(key=lambda x: x[1] or 9999)
for fuel, yr, val in onset:
    print(f"  {fuel:25s} first non-zero: {yr}  (start value: {val:.2f} TWh)" if val else f"  {fuel:25s} all zero")

The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Fuel onset years — when each source first appears in the global mix
raw_evidence.content: The OWID series records the first year each primary-energy source registers a non-zero global contribution: coal (1800, but actually centuries earlier in England — the file just starts at 1800), oil (1870, 6 TWh), natural gas and hydropower (both 1890, 33 and 39 TWh respectively), nuclear (1965, 71 TWh — eleven years after Obninsk's grid connection), wind (1978, 0.01 TWh, essentially noise from California's first commercial turbines), and solar (1983, 0.01 TWh, from early grid-tied photovoltaic experiments). The clustering of new sources at 1890 (oil scaling, hydro emerging) and 1965 (nuclear, biofuels, geothermal) matches the textbook periodisation of the 2nd and 3rd industrial revolutions almost exactly.

The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

sources.title: Second Industrial Revolution — Wikipedia
facts: The Second Industrial Revolution spanned approximately 1870 to 1914.
It was built on steelmaking, electrical energy, and chemical processes that enabled mass production.

sources.title: Joel Mokyr — The Second Industrial Revolution, 1870-1914

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Global energy mix 1800-2024 — the spine stacked-area data
raw_evidence.content: The core__global-energy-by-source.csv file gives the world's primary-energy supply by source from 1800 through 2024, in TWh/year on the OWID substitution-method convention. In 1800 the entire global energy supply was 5,653 TWh, of which 5,556 TWh (98.3%) was traditional biomass (wood, dung, peat) and 97 TWh (1.7%) was coal — essentially the energy mix of antiquity, with coal as a thin sliver visible mainly in Britain. By 2024 the total was 186,383 TWh — a 33-fold increase over 224 years — with traditional biomass having shrunk to 11,111 TWh (6.0%) and ten distinct other sources now in play. The transformation is not one revolution but four stacked on top of each other: each new fuel was added without the previous one being retired.

raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Global energy mix 1800-2024 — the spine stacked-area data
raw_evidence.content: The core__global-energy-by-source.csv file gives the world's primary-energy supply by source from 1800 through 2024, in TWh/year on the OWID substitution-method convention. In 1800 the entire global energy supply was 5,653 TWh, of which 5,556 TWh (98.3%) was traditional biomass (wood, dung, peat) and 97 TWh (1.7%) was coal — essentially the energy mix of antiquity, with coal as a thin sliver visible mainly in Britain. By 2024 the total was 186,383 TWh — a 33-fold increase over 224 years — with traditional biomass having shrunk to 11,111 TWh (6.0%) and ten distinct other sources now in play. The transformation is not one revolution but four stacked on top of each other: each new fuel was added without the previous one being retired.

raw_evidence.label: Fuel onset years — when each source first appears in the global mix
raw_evidence.content: The OWID series records the first year each primary-energy source registers a non-zero global contribution: coal (1800, but actually centuries earlier in England — the file just starts at 1800), oil (1870, 6 TWh), natural gas and hydropower (both 1890, 33 and 39 TWh respectively), nuclear (1965, 71 TWh — eleven years after Obninsk's grid connection), wind (1978, 0.01 TWh, essentially noise from California's first commercial turbines), and solar (1983, 0.01 TWh, from early grid-tied photovoltaic experiments). The clustering of new sources at 1890 (oil scaling, hydro emerging) and 1965 (nuclear, biofuels, geothermal) matches the textbook periodisation of the 2nd and 3rd industrial revolutions almost exactly.

raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Global energy mix 1800-2024 — the spine stacked-area data
raw_evidence.content: The core__global-energy-by-source.csv file gives the world's primary-energy supply by source from 1800 through 2024, in TWh/year on the OWID substitution-method convention. In 1800 the entire global energy supply was 5,653 TWh, of which 5,556 TWh (98.3%) was traditional biomass (wood, dung, peat) and 97 TWh (1.7%) was coal — essentially the energy mix of antiquity, with coal as a thin sliver visible mainly in Britain. raw_evidence.label: Fuel onset years — when each source first appears in the global mix
raw_evidence.content: The OWID series records the first year each primary-energy source registers a non-zero global contribution: coal (1800, but actually centuries earlier in England — the file just starts at 1800), oil (1870, 6 TWh), natural gas and hydropower (both 1890, 33 and 39 TWh respectively), nuclear (1965, 71 TWh — eleven years after Obninsk's grid connection), wind (1978, 0.01 TWh, essentially noise from California's first commercial turbines), and solar (1983, 0.01 TWh, from early grid-tied photovoltaic experiments). raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

Newcomen's coal-powered steam engine dates from 1712.
James Watt's improved version with a separate water condenser was developed in the 1760s.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: 1st industrial revolution: coal + steam (1760-1840, Britain)
raw_evidence.content: The first industrial revolution is conventionally dated c. 1760-1840 and centred on Britain, where Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712) and especially James Watt's separate-condenser improvement (patented 1769, commercial 1776) made coal-fired mechanical power economically viable at scale. By the early 1700s deforestation had pushed Britain off charcoal and toward coal for heat and metallurgy; the engine then created the demand that justified extracting coal at far greater volumes. The new mechanised textile mills, iron furnaces, and pumping engines all consumed coal directly. Britain's pre-industrial fuel base was overwhelmingly biomass (firewood, dung, peat); the revolution's signature wasn't "new technology" alone but the conversion of an entire economy to a fossil substrate — coal — that previously only specialists used. The English coal column in the Bank of England's millennium dataset shows industrial coal use was already nontrivial in England before James Watt, so the steam engine should be read as accelerating an existing fuel transition rather than starting one from zero.

raw_evidence.label: 2nd industrial revolution: oil + electricity + steel (1870-1914)
raw_evidence.content: The second industrial revolution, c. 1870-1914, was the period when oil entered the global energy mix and electricity became the dominant carrier of mechanical work over distance. Three innovations stand out: the Bessemer steel process (1856; supplying ~80% of all steel between 1880 and 1895), the internal combustion engine, and the electrification of factories and cities through dynamos, motors, and the incandescent bulb. Oil's first commercial volumes were refined for kerosene lighting, not transport — the gasoline market followed the automobile. Hydropower entered roughly in parallel: large-scale hydroelectric stations come online from the 1880s-1900s and feed the new electric grids. The era's per-capita energy consumption climbed sharply in the industrialising countries, and its CO2 footprint shows the steepest pre-WWI climb in the OWID Global Carbon Project series. Economic historian Joel Mokyr characterises this period as a genuine "technological revolution" distinct from the first — not a continuation of steam, but a substitution of new energy carriers (electricity, oil) for the old one.

raw_evidence.label: 3rd industrial revolution: nuclear + natural gas + digital (1950-2000)
raw_evidence.content: The third industrial revolution, c. 1950-2000, paired a new primary-energy entrant — civilian nuclear fission — with the fastest-growing fossil fuel of the era, natural gas, and the digital substrate that came to define the period: semiconductors and computers. The first grid-connected civilian nuclear plant was Obninsk in the Soviet Union (commissioned 27 June 1954, ~6 MW); the first full-scale commercial reactor was Shippingport, Pennsylvania (first criticality 2 December 1957, first power 18 December 1957). Natural gas, previously flared at oil wells, became economic over long distances once high-pressure pipeline networks expanded after WWII; it grew faster than coal or oil through the second half of the 20th century. In parallel, Moore's Law observed that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly doubled every two years — the OWID transistors-per-chip series captures this from the Intel 4004 (1971) onwards. That density curve is what made digital computing affordable, then ubiquitous, and ultimately what made training large neural networks even imaginable by the 2010s.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Global energy mix 1800-2024 — the spine stacked-area data
raw_evidence.content: The core__global-energy-by-source.csv file gives the world's primary-energy supply by source from 1800 through 2024, in TWh/year on the OWID substitution-method convention. In 1800 the entire global energy supply was 5,653 TWh, of which 5,556 TWh (98.3%) was traditional biomass (wood, dung, peat) and 97 TWh (1.7%) was coal — essentially the energy mix of antiquity, with coal as a thin sliver visible mainly in Britain. By 2024 the total was 186,383 TWh — a 33-fold increase over 224 years — with traditional biomass having shrunk to 11,111 TWh (6.0%) and ten distinct other sources now in play. The transformation is not one revolution but four stacked on top of each other: each new fuel was added without the previous one being retired.

raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: Total fossil share peaked at 81.6% in 1973 — and is still 76% today
raw_evidence.content: Combining coal, oil, and natural gas: the fossil share of global primary energy peaked at 81.63% in 1973 (the year of the OPEC oil shock, when fossil energy reached its highest dominance ever in absolute share terms) and has declined only modestly to 76.41% in 2024 — a drop of just ~5 percentage points in 51 years. In absolute TWh, fossil consumption has grown from 53,387 TWh (1970) to 142,421 TWh (2024) — nearly 3x more. So although renewables and nuclear have prevented the fossil share from continuing to expand, they have not actually pushed the world's fossil consumption down: every year of the 21st century has seen more fossil burning than the year before, with the partial exception of pandemic-affected 2020.

Its share then fell as oil and gas took share, dropping to 22.45% by 2000 before partially recovering to 24.60% by 2024 (Chinese industrial growth being the dominant cause). Crucially, coal's share has fallen but its absolute consumption has not: 1910 = 9,136 TWh; 2024 = 45,851 TWh. Coal hit its absolute volume peak in 2024 — the most recent year in the dataset. Despite a century of cleaner alternatives being available, we burn five times as much coal now as at the supposed apex of the coal age. This is the empirical case for Smil's slow-transition thesis: even after a fuel loses share, displacement of absolute volume happens decades later, if at all.

raw_evidence.label: Coal trajectory — share peaked 1910, absolute volume still rising in 2024
raw_evidence.content: Coal's share of global primary energy peaked at 55.22% in 1910 — the high-water mark of the steam-and-railway era. Its share then fell as oil and gas took share, dropping to 22.45% by 2000 before partially recovering to 24.60% by 2024 (Chinese industrial growth being the dominant cause). Crucially, coal's share has fallen but its absolute consumption has not: 1910 = 9,136 TWh; 2024 = 45,851 TWh. Coal hit its absolute volume peak in 2024 — the most recent year in the dataset. Despite a century of cleaner alternatives being available, we burn five times as much coal now as at the supposed apex of the coal age. This is the empirical case for Smil's slow-transition thesis: even after a fuel loses share, displacement of absolute volume happens decades later, if at all.

raw_evidence.label: Total fossil share peaked at 81.6% in 1973 — and is still 76% today
raw_evidence.content: Combining coal, oil, and natural gas: the fossil share of global primary energy peaked at 81.63% in 1973 (the year of the OPEC oil shock, when fossil energy reached its highest dominance ever in absolute share terms) and has declined only modestly to 76.41% in 2024 — a drop of just ~5 percentage points in 51 years. In absolute TWh, fossil consumption has grown from 53,387 TWh (1970) to 142,421 TWh (2024) — nearly 3x more. So although renewables and nuclear have prevented the fossil share from continuing to expand, they have not actually pushed the world's fossil consumption down: every year of the 21st century has seen more fossil burning than the year before, with the partial exception of pandemic-affected 2020.

raw_evidence.label: Caveat: substitution vs physical-content primary-energy accounting
raw_evidence.content: The spine file core__global-energy-by-source.csv uses Our World in Data's substitution-method primary-energy accounting. The substitution method divides non-fossil electricity (nuclear, hydro, solar, wind) by a thermal-efficiency factor — effectively asking "how many TWh of fossil fuel would a thermal plant have burned to produce this much non-fossil electricity?" — so nuclear and renewables get scaled up to fossil-equivalent terms. The IEA, Eurostat, the UN, and the US EIA now use the physical-content method, which counts the actual joules of electricity delivered without the thermal-equivalent inflation. The two methods produce significantly different shares for renewables and nuclear: substitution makes them look larger; physical content makes them look smaller. Either is defensible; they're answering different questions. The blog should call this out when comparing OWID numbers to IEA-style ones, so a reader who has seen "renewables are 30% of energy" from one source and "renewables are 15%" from another doesn't think one of them is wrong.

raw_evidence.label: World CO2 emissions 1750-2024 — the 4,148x cumulative climb
raw_evidence.content: Annual world CO2 emissions in 1750 were 9.3 million tonnes — most of it from English coal. By 2024 the global total was 38.6 billion tonnes per year — a multiplier of 4,148x over 274 years. The acceleration tracks the energy revolutions almost cleanly: 0.03 Gt in 1800 (start of coal era), 1.96 Gt in 1900 (after the steam-railway boom), 5.93 Gt in 1950 (after WWII), 14.90 Gt in 1970 (post-war demand), and 38.60 Gt in 2024 (peak fossil consumption). Three small kinks in the curve are visible: a brief decline 2008-2009 (financial crisis), another 2014-2016 (Chinese coal slowdown), and a sharp pandemic drop in 2020 followed by a rebound. None of the structural inflection points — the rise of nuclear, the post-2010 renewables takeoff — show up as breaks in the line. The world's CO2 trajectory is dictated by absolute fossil consumption, and that has never stopped growing.

raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: World CO2 emissions 1750-2024 — the 4,148x cumulative climb
raw_evidence.content: Annual world CO2 emissions in 1750 were 9.3 million tonnes — most of it from English coal. By 2024 the global total was 38.6 billion tonnes per year — a multiplier of 4,148x over 274 years. The acceleration tracks the energy revolutions almost cleanly: 0.03 Gt in 1800 (start of coal era), 1.96 Gt in 1900 (after the steam-railway boom), 5.93 Gt in 1950 (after WWII), 14.90 Gt in 1970 (post-war demand), and 38.60 Gt in 2024 (peak fossil consumption). Three small kinks in the curve are visible: a brief decline 2008-2009 (financial crisis), another 2014-2016 (Chinese coal slowdown), and a sharp pandemic drop in 2020 followed by a rebound. None of the structural inflection points — the rise of nuclear, the post-2010 renewables takeoff — show up as breaks in the line. The world's CO2 trajectory is dictated by absolute fossil consumption, and that has never stopped growing.

raw_evidence.label: Decoupling check — CO2 per TWh non-biomass energy has fallen ~36% since 1850
raw_evidence.content: Dividing world CO2 emissions by world non-biomass primary energy gives the carbon intensity of modern energy: roughly 346,000 tonnes CO2 per TWh in 1850 (almost pure coal), falling to 220,000 t/TWh by 2024 — a ~36% decline over 174 years. The decline is not nothing: it reflects oil and gas being less carbon-intensive than coal, and nuclear and renewables being effectively zero. But it is decoupling at glacial pace. To zero out CO2 we need ~95%+ decline in carbon intensity OR a contraction in fossil volume, and the actual rate of intensity decline is on the order of ~0.3% per year. The 4th-revolution renewables additions are the first big step-down in the historical trend, but they are also being chased by AI-compute electricity demand that wants the additional clean capacity for itself.
