# --- ana_07: Decoupling check — CO2 per TWh non-biomass primary energy ---
print("\n=== ana_07 ===")
mix = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "core__global-energy-by-source.csv")
fossils = ["Coal", "Oil", "Natural gas"]
non_biomass_cols = ["Coal", "Oil", "Natural gas", "Hydropower", "Nuclear", "Solar", "Wind", "Modern biofuels", "Other renewables"]
mix["non_biomass_TWh"] = mix[non_biomass_cols].sum(axis=1)
mix["fossil_TWh"] = mix[fossils].sum(axis=1)
merged = world.merge(mix[["Year", "non_biomass_TWh", "fossil_TWh"]], on="Year", how="inner")
merged["CO2_per_TWh_nonbiomass"] = merged.CO2 / merged.non_biomass_TWh  # tonnes / TWh
merged["CO2_per_TWh_fossil"] = merged.CO2 / merged.fossil_TWh
print("Year | World CO2 (Gt) | NonBio TWh | CO2/TWh_nonbio (t/TWh) | CO2/TWh_fossil (t/TWh)")
for y in [1850, 1900, 1950, 1970, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2024]:
    r = merged[merged.Year == y]
    if not r.empty:
        a, b, c, d = r.CO2.iloc[0]/1e9, r.non_biomass_TWh.iloc[0], r.CO2_per_TWh_nonbiomass.iloc[0], r.CO2_per_TWh_fossil.iloc[0]
        print(f"  {y}  {a:6.2f}        {b:8.0f}       {c:10.0f}             {d:10.0f}")

raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: Caveat: substitution vs physical-content primary-energy accounting
raw_evidence.content: The spine file core__global-energy-by-source.csv uses Our World in Data's substitution-method primary-energy accounting. The substitution method divides non-fossil electricity (nuclear, hydro, solar, wind) by a thermal-efficiency factor — effectively asking "how many TWh of fossil fuel would a thermal plant have burned to produce this much non-fossil electricity?" — so nuclear and renewables get scaled up to fossil-equivalent terms. The IEA, Eurostat, the UN, and the US EIA now use the physical-content method, which counts the actual joules of electricity delivered without the thermal-equivalent inflation. The two methods produce significantly different shares for renewables and nuclear: substitution makes them look larger; physical content makes them look smaller. Either is defensible; they're answering different questions. The blog should call this out when comparing OWID numbers to IEA-style ones, so a reader who has seen "renewables are 30% of energy" from one source and "renewables are 15%" from another doesn't think one of them is wrong.

raw_evidence.label: Top 15 cumulative CO2 emitters since 1750 — US alone is 24%
raw_evidence.content: Summing every country's annual emissions from 1750 to 2024 produces a cumulative responsibility table that runs counter to the present-day flow ranking. The United States is the cumulative leader at 434.9 Gt (24.1% of all country-attributed CO2), more than 1.5x China's 285.1 Gt (15.8%) despite China's higher current emissions. The next tier — Russia (122.8 Gt), Germany (95.1), the United Kingdom (80.1), and Japan (69.6) — are all early-industrial economies whose 19th- and 20th-century emissions still dominate the running total. India, despite being the world's #3 current emitter, sits at 7th cumulatively (66.1 Gt, 3.66%) because its industrial era started late. Together the top 15 countries account for 76.7% of the total 1.80 trillion tonnes of cumulative country-attributed CO2 since 1750.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: Top cumulative CO2 emitters 1750-2024 ---
print("\n=== ana_08 ===")
# Drop aggregates (those without Code or with all-caps non-ISO3 codes)
real = co2.copy()
# Keep only rows with a 3-letter Code (real countries) — exclude regions / aggregates
real = real[real.Code.notna() & real.Code.str.match(r"^[A-Z]{3}$") & (real.Code != "OWID_WRL")]
cum = real.groupby("Entity").CO2.sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
total_cum = cum.sum()
print(f"Cumulative country-attributed CO2 1750-2024: {total_cum/1e12:.2f} Tt (trillion tonnes)")
print("\nTop 15 cumulative emitters:")
top15 = cum.head(15)
for ent, val in top15.items():
    pct = val / total_cum * 100
    print(f"  {ent:30s}  {val/1e9:8.1f} Gt   {pct:5.2f}%")
top15_share = top15.sum() / total_cum * 100

# --- ana_08: Top cumulative CO2 emitters 1750-2024 ---

raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: Caveat: substitution vs physical-content primary-energy accounting
raw_evidence.content: The spine file core__global-energy-by-source.csv uses Our World in Data's substitution-method primary-energy accounting. The substitution method divides non-fossil electricity (nuclear, hydro, solar, wind) by a thermal-efficiency factor — effectively asking "how many TWh of fossil fuel would a thermal plant have burned to produce this much non-fossil electricity?" — so nuclear and renewables get scaled up to fossil-equivalent terms. The IEA, Eurostat, the UN, and the US EIA now use the physical-content method, which counts the actual joules of electricity delivered without the thermal-equivalent inflation. The two methods produce significantly different shares for renewables and nuclear: substitution makes them look larger; physical content makes them look smaller. Either is defensible; they're answering different questions. The blog should call this out when comparing OWID numbers to IEA-style ones, so a reader who has seen "renewables are 30% of energy" from one source and "renewables are 15%" from another doesn't think one of them is wrong.

raw_evidence.label: World CO2 emissions 1750-2024 — the 4,148x cumulative climb
raw_evidence.content: Annual world CO2 emissions in 1750 were 9.3 million tonnes — most of it from English coal. By 2024 the global total was 38.6 billion tonnes per year — a multiplier of 4,148x over 274 years. The acceleration tracks the energy revolutions almost cleanly: 0.03 Gt in 1800 (start of coal era), 1.96 Gt in 1900 (after the steam-railway boom), 5.93 Gt in 1950 (after WWII), 14.90 Gt in 1970 (post-war demand), and 38.60 Gt in 2024 (peak fossil consumption). Three small kinks in the curve are visible: a brief decline 2008-2009 (financial crisis), another 2014-2016 (Chinese coal slowdown), and a sharp pandemic drop in 2020 followed by a rebound. None of the structural inflection points — the rise of nuclear, the post-2010 renewables takeoff — show up as breaks in the line. The world's CO2 trajectory is dictated by absolute fossil consumption, and that has never stopped growing.

raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: World CO2 emissions 1750-2024 — the 4,148x cumulative climb
raw_evidence.content: Annual world CO2 emissions in 1750 were 9.3 million tonnes — most of it from English coal. By 2024 the global total was 38.6 billion tonnes per year — a multiplier of 4,148x over 274 years. The acceleration tracks the energy revolutions almost cleanly: 0.03 Gt in 1800 (start of coal era), 1.96 Gt in 1900 (after the steam-railway boom), 5.93 Gt in 1950 (after WWII), 14.90 Gt in 1970 (post-war demand), and 38.60 Gt in 2024 (peak fossil consumption). Three small kinks in the curve are visible: a brief decline 2008-2009 (financial crisis), another 2014-2016 (Chinese coal slowdown), and a sharp pandemic drop in 2020 followed by a rebound. None of the structural inflection points — the rise of nuclear, the post-2010 renewables takeoff — show up as breaks in the line. The world's CO2 trajectory is dictated by absolute fossil consumption, and that has never stopped growing.

raw_evidence.label: Top 15 cumulative CO2 emitters since 1750 — US alone is 24%
raw_evidence.content: Summing every country's annual emissions from 1750 to 2024 produces a cumulative responsibility table that runs counter to the present-day flow ranking. The United States is the cumulative leader at 434.9 Gt (24.1% of all country-attributed CO2), more than 1.5x China's 285.1 Gt (15.8%) despite China's higher current emissions. The next tier — Russia (122.8 Gt), Germany (95.1), the United Kingdom (80.1), and Japan (69.6) — are all early-industrial economies whose 19th- and 20th-century emissions still dominate the running total. India, despite being the world's #3 current emitter, sits at 7th cumulatively (66.1 Gt, 3.66%) because its industrial era started late. Together the top 15 countries account for 76.7% of the total 1.80 trillion tonnes of cumulative country-attributed CO2 since 1750.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: Top cumulative CO2 emitters 1750-2024 ---
print("\n=== ana_08 ===")
# Drop aggregates (those without Code or with all-caps non-ISO3 codes)
real = co2.copy()
# Keep only rows with a 3-letter Code (real countries) — exclude regions / aggregates
real = real[real.Code.notna() & real.Code.str.match(r"^[A-Z]{3}$") & (real.Code != "OWID_WRL")]
cum = real.groupby("Entity").CO2.sum().sort_values(ascending=False)
total_cum = cum.sum()
print(f"Cumulative country-attributed CO2 1750-2024: {total_cum/1e12:.2f} Tt (trillion tonnes)")
print("\nTop 15 cumulative emitters:")
top15 = cum.head(15)
for ent, val in top15.items():
    pct = val / total_cum * 100
    print(f"  {ent:30s}  {val/1e9:8.1f} Gt   {pct:5.2f}%")
top15_share = top15.sum() / total_cum * 100

raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: Caveat: substitution vs physical-content primary-energy accounting
raw_evidence.content: The spine file core__global-energy-by-source.csv uses Our World in Data's substitution-method primary-energy accounting. The substitution method divides non-fossil electricity (nuclear, hydro, solar, wind) by a thermal-efficiency factor — effectively asking "how many TWh of fossil fuel would a thermal plant have burned to produce this much non-fossil electricity?" — so nuclear and renewables get scaled up to fossil-equivalent terms. The IEA, Eurostat, the UN, and the US EIA now use the physical-content method, which counts the actual joules of electricity delivered without the thermal-equivalent inflation. The two methods produce significantly different shares for renewables and nuclear: substitution makes them look larger; physical content makes them look smaller. Either is defensible; they're answering different questions. The blog should call this out when comparing OWID numbers to IEA-style ones, so a reader who has seen "renewables are 30% of energy" from one source and "renewables are 15%" from another doesn't think one of them is wrong.

raw_evidence.label: Top 15 cumulative CO2 emitters since 1750 — US alone is 24%
raw_evidence.content: Summing every country's annual emissions from 1750 to 2024 produces a cumulative responsibility table that runs counter to the present-day flow ranking. The United States is the cumulative leader at 434.9 Gt (24.1% of all country-attributed CO2), more than 1.5x China's 285.1 Gt (15.8%) despite China's higher current emissions. The next tier — Russia (122.8 Gt), Germany (95.1), the United Kingdom (80.1), and Japan (69.6) — are all early-industrial economies whose 19th- and 20th-century emissions still dominate the running total. India, despite being the world's #3 current emitter, sits at 7th cumulatively (66.1 Gt, 3.66%) because its industrial era started late. Together the top 15 countries account for 76.7% of the total 1.80 trillion tonnes of cumulative country-attributed CO2 since 1750.

print("\n=== ana_08 ===")

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Solar + wind: from 11 TWh (1990) to 11,275 TWh (2024) — a 1,000x jump
raw_evidence.content: Solar and wind together generated 11.2 TWh of primary energy globally in 1990 — about 0.01% of the world's energy supply. By 2024 they produced 11,275 TWh, a thousand-fold increase, and accounted for 6.05% of primary energy (about 15% of electricity, since they only show up in the electric sector). The doubling has not slowed: 2010 (990 TWh) -> 2015 (2,755 TWh) -> 2020 (6,057 TWh) -> 2024 (11,275 TWh) is a near-perfect doubling every ~5 years. Within the pair, solar caught wind in 2024 (5,151 vs 6,124 TWh) after lagging since the 1980s — solar PV is now the world's fastest-deploying source of new generation, per IEA Renewables 2024.
raw_evidence.code:
print("\n=== ana_05 ===")
solar_wind = df["Solar"] + df["Wind"]
sw_share = (solar_wind / df["Total"]) * 100
for y in [1990, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2024]:
    row = df[df.Year == y]
    if not row.empty:
        i = row.index[0]
        print(f"  {y}: Solar+Wind = {solar_wind.iloc[i]:7.1f} TWh ({sw_share.iloc[i]:5.2f}% of primary)  [solar {df.Solar.iloc[i]:.1f}, wind {df.Wind.iloc[i]:.1f}]")
raw_evidence.output:

  2024: Solar+Wind = 11275.0 TWh (6.05%)

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Per-capita energy: China 2024 still below US 1965
raw_evidence.content: Per-capita energy consumption tells the convergence story that aggregate volume hides. In 1965 the United States consumed 73,802 kWh per person; by 2024 it was 76,800 kWh — essentially flat across 60 years of population and GDP growth. China, by contrast, went from 2,124 kWh/capita in 1965 to 34,514 kWh/capita in 2024 — a 16x jump that crossed the EU average (35,318 kWh/cap in 2024) only narrowly. Crucially, China's 2024 per-capita consumption is still only 47% of the US 1965 level. India (7,813 kWh/cap in 2024) is at roughly 10% of the US 1965 level. Africa (4,055 kWh/cap in 2024) has barely moved since 1965 (2,228 kWh/cap). The world average sits at 21,654 kWh/cap in 2024, dragged up by China's industrialisation but still less than a third of US-level demand. If the rest of the world reaches even half the US per-capita level by 2050, total world energy will need to grow at a pace none of the renewables-buildout scenarios currently model.

raw_evidence.label: 4th industrial revolution: renewables + AI compute (2010-present)
raw_evidence.content: The framing of a "Fourth Industrial Revolution" was popularised by Klaus Schwab (World Economic Forum) in 2016, describing the convergence of artificial intelligence, robotics, IoT, and biotechnology that blurs the physical, digital, and biological worlds. The periodisation is contested — critics argue it's a marketing label rather than a discrete technological break — but two empirical regularities ground it as more than rhetoric. First, solar and wind, negligible in 2000, supplied ~15% of global electricity generation by 2024 (up about 13 percentage points since 2010), and the IEA forecasts ~30% by 2030 from wind+solar alone. Second, frontier AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010 — a 4.4x annual growth that no prior energy-intensive workload has matched. The two trends collide on the electricity grid: data centres consumed ~415 TWh globally in 2024 (about 1.5% of world electricity) and the IEA projects ~945 TWh by 2030, with hyperscaler campuses now routinely contracting for 100 MW to >1 GW of dedicated capacity. The 4th industrial revolution's signature fuel question is therefore unsettled: it's running on whichever electrons the grid can spare, and the grid is built for an earlier era.

raw_evidence.label: Per-capita energy: China 2024 still below US 1965
raw_evidence.content: Per-capita energy consumption tells the convergence story that aggregate volume hides. In 1965 the United States consumed 73,802 kWh per person; by 2024 it was 76,800 kWh — essentially flat across 60 years of population and GDP growth. China, by contrast, went from 2,124 kWh/capita in 1965 to 34,514 kWh/capita in 2024 — a 16x jump that crossed the EU average (35,318 kWh/cap in 2024) only narrowly. Crucially, China's 2024 per-capita consumption is still only 47% of the US 1965 level. India (7,813 kWh/cap in 2024) is at roughly 10% of the US 1965 level. Africa (4,055 kWh/cap in 2024) has barely moved since 1965 (2,228 kWh/cap). The world average sits at 21,654 kWh/cap in 2024, dragged up by China's industrialisation but still less than a third of US-level demand. If the rest of the world reaches even half the US per-capita level by 2050, total world energy will need to grow at a pace none of the renewables-buildout scenarios currently model.

for y in [1965, 1980, 2000, 2010, 2020, 2024]:
    if y in tab.index:

        print(f"  {y}: " + ", ".join(f"{ent}={int(v) if pd.notna(v) else 'NA'}" for ent, v in row.items()))

print(f"China 2024 / US 1965: {cn_2024/us_1965:.2f}x")

raw_evidence.label: AI training compute is doubling every ~6 months
raw_evidence.content: Since 2010, the training compute used to create notable AI models has been growing at roughly 4.4x per year — a doubling time of approximately 6 months. This is Epoch AI's headline finding from their AI Models database (the same database that supplies the core__ai-notable-models.csv file in this bundle, with 1,018 models from 1950 to 2026). The growth is sourced from three multipliers compounding together: more chips deployed in parallel, longer training runs, and newer accelerators with higher per-chip throughput. Frontier training-compute spending is doubling roughly every 8 months; power draw per frontier run is doubling annually. For context, the doubling time across all machine-learning history before 2010 was much slower (~20 months in the original 2018 OpenAI analysis). The post-2010 acceleration is the empirical anchor for the "4th industrial revolution as compute revolution" framing.

raw_evidence.label: Moore's Law slowdown — the compute side of the 4th-revolution story
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law — Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly double every two years — drove the third industrial revolution and underwrote the fourth. The OWID transistors-per-chip series in this bundle (1971-2021, 39 data points, Intel 4004 → modern multi-core CPUs) traces the long arc. But the cadence has slowed: Intel's then-CEO Brian Krzanich publicly conceded in 2015 that the cadence had moved "closer to two and a half years than two," and industry observers describe the post-2010 transistor-density growth as linear rather than exponential. Continued advances now come from EUV lithography, gate-all-around transistors, and 2nm-class processes (Intel 18A, TSMC N2, Samsung 2nm), but each new node costs far more and adds less. The interpretive hook for the AI-compute story is sharp: at the moment AI training compute started doubling every six months (2010 onwards), the per-chip transistor density underneath it started growing more slowly. The compute curve is steeper than ever, but the chips are no longer carrying it — the multiplier is now parallelism, runtime, and raw electricity.

raw_evidence.label: Moore's Law slowdown — the compute side of the 4th-revolution story
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law — Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly double every two years — drove the third industrial revolution and underwrote the fourth. The OWID transistors-per-chip series in this bundle (1971-2021, 39 data points, Intel 4004 → modern multi-core CPUs) traces the long arc. But the cadence has slowed: Intel's then-CEO Brian Krzanich publicly conceded in 2015 that the cadence had moved "closer to two and a half years than two," and industry observers describe the post-2010 transistor-density growth as linear rather than exponential. Continued advances now come from EUV lithography, gate-all-around transistors, and 2nm-class processes (Intel 18A, TSMC N2, Samsung 2nm), but each new node costs far more and adds less. The interpretive hook for the AI-compute story is sharp: at the moment AI training compute started doubling every six months (2010 onwards), the per-chip transistor density underneath it started growing more slowly. The compute curve is steeper than ever, but the chips are no longer carrying it — the multiplier is now parallelism, runtime, and raw electricity.

raw_evidence.label: Moore's Law: transistor density grew 25 million-fold, 1971-2021
raw_evidence.content: The OWID transistors-per-chip file traces 39 named microprocessors from the Intel 4004 (1971, 2,308 transistors) to a 2021 frontier chip with 58.2 billion transistors — a 25-million-fold increase over 50 years. Fitting log-linear trends, the doubling time is 23.5 months pre-2010 and 26.5 months post-2010 — confirming Moore's Law has slowed modestly but not stopped. That ~10% slowdown in the per-chip curve coexists with the post-2010 acceleration in AI training compute (5.7-month doubling), which means roughly 4-5x of the AI-compute growth must be coming from parallelism (more chips per run) and longer runtimes rather than per-chip improvements. The transistors-per-chip series is well-curated but coarse: 39 points across 50 years means each step is a specific named landmark chip, not a continuous benchmark. Treat the trendline as illustrative rather than a precise per-chip-year metric.

print("=== ana_15 ===")
print(f"Rows: {len(m)}; Year range: {int(m.Year.min())}-{int(m.Year.max())}")

for y in [1971, 1985, 2000, 2010, 2015, 2021]:
    near = m[m.Year == y]
    if not near.empty:
        print(f"  {y}: {int(near.transistors.iloc[0]):,} transistors")
print(f"  ALL: 1971 first = {int(m.transistors.iloc[0]):,}; 2021 last = {int(m.transistors.iloc[-1]):,}")
mult = m.transistors.iloc[-1] / m.transistors.iloc[0]
print(f"  Multiplier 1971->2021: {mult:.2e}x")

# Doubling time pre-2010 vs post-2010
pre = m[m.Year < 2010]
post = m[m.Year >= 2010]

def doubling(df_):
    b, a = np.polyfit(df_.Year.astype(float), np.log10(df_.transistors), 1)
    dt = np.log10(2) / b if b > 0 else float("inf")
    return b, dt

if len(pre) >= 2:
    b_pre, dt_pre = doubling(pre)
    print(f"Pre-2010 ({len(pre)} pts): log10 slope = {b_pre:.4f}/yr  =>  doubling time = {dt_pre*12:.1f} months")
if len(post) >= 2:
    b_post, dt_post = doubling(post)

raw_evidence.label: Moore's Law slowdown — the compute side of the 4th-revolution story
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law — Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly double every two years — drove the third industrial revolution and underwrote the fourth. The OWID transistors-per-chip series in this bundle (1971-2021, 39 data points, Intel 4004 → modern multi-core CPUs) traces the long arc. But the cadence has slowed: Intel's then-CEO Brian Krzanich publicly conceded in 2015 that the cadence had moved "closer to two and a half years than two," and industry observers describe the post-2010 transistor-density growth as linear rather than exponential. Continued advances now come from EUV lithography, gate-all-around transistors, and 2nm-class processes (Intel 18A, TSMC N2, Samsung 2nm), but each new node costs far more and adds less. The interpretive hook for the AI-compute story is sharp: at the moment AI training compute started doubling every six months (2010 onwards), the per-chip transistor density underneath it started growing more slowly. The compute curve is steeper than ever, but the chips are no longer carrying it — the multiplier is now parallelism, runtime, and raw electricity.

The interpretive hook for the AI-compute story is sharp: at the moment AI training compute started doubling every six months (2010 onwards), the per-chip transistor density underneath it started growing more slowly. The compute curve is steeper than ever, but the chips are no longer carrying it — the multiplier is now parallelism, runtime, and raw electricity.

raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law — Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly double every two years — drove the third industrial revolution and underwrote the fourth. The OWID transistors-per-chip series in this bundle (1971-2021, 39 data points, Intel 4004 → modern multi-core CPUs) traces the long arc. But the cadence has slowed: Intel's then-CEO Brian Krzanich publicly conceded in 2015 that the cadence had moved "closer to two and a half years than two," and industry observers describe the post-2010 transistor-density growth as linear rather than exponential. Continued advances now come from EUV lithography, gate-all-around transistors, and 2nm-class processes (Intel 18A, TSMC N2, Samsung 2nm), but each new node costs far more and adds less. The interpretive hook for the AI-compute story is sharp: at the moment AI training compute started doubling every six months (2010 onwards), the per-chip transistor density underneath it started growing more slowly. The compute curve is steeper than ever, but the chips are no longer carrying it — the multiplier is now parallelism, runtime, and raw electricity.

raw_evidence.label: Moore's Law: transistor density grew 25 million-fold, 1971-2021
raw_evidence.content: The OWID transistors-per-chip file traces 39 named microprocessors from the Intel 4004 (1971, 2,308 transistors) to a 2021 frontier chip with 58.2 billion transistors — a 25-million-fold increase over 50 years. Fitting log-linear trends, the doubling time is 23.5 months pre-2010 and 26.5 months post-2010 — confirming Moore's Law has slowed modestly but not stopped. That ~10% slowdown in the per-chip curve coexists with the post-2010 acceleration in AI training compute (5.7-month doubling), which means roughly 4-5x of the AI-compute growth must be coming from parallelism (more chips per run) and longer runtimes rather than per-chip improvements. The transistors-per-chip series is well-curated but coarse: 39 points across 50 years means each step is a specific named landmark chip, not a continuous benchmark. Treat the trendline as illustrative rather than a precise per-chip-year metric.

    near = m[m.Year == y]
    if not near.empty:
        print(f"  {y}: {int(near.transistors.iloc[0]):,} transistors")
print(f"  ALL: 1971 first = {int(m.transistors.iloc[0]):,}; 2021 last = {int(m.transistors.iloc[-1]):,}")
mult = m.transistors.iloc[-1] / m.transistors.iloc[0]
print(f"  Multiplier 1971->2021: {mult:.2e}x")

# Doubling time pre-2010 vs post-2010
pre = m[m.Year < 2010]
post = m[m.Year >= 2010]

def doubling(df_):
    b, a = np.polyfit(df_.Year.astype(float), np.log10(df_.transistors), 1)
    dt = np.log10(2) / b if b > 0 else float("inf")
    return b, dt

if len(pre) >= 2:
    b_pre, dt_pre = doubling(pre)
    print(f"Pre-2010 ({len(pre)} pts): log10 slope = {b_pre:.4f}/yr  =>  doubling time = {dt_pre*12:.1f} months")
if len(post) >= 2:
    b_post, dt_post = doubling(post)

raw_evidence.label: AI training compute is doubling every ~6 months
raw_evidence.content: Since 2010, the training compute used to create notable AI models has been growing at roughly 4.4x per year — a doubling time of approximately 6 months. This is Epoch AI's headline finding from their AI Models database (the same database that supplies the core__ai-notable-models.csv file in this bundle, with 1,018 models from 1950 to 2026). The growth is sourced from three multipliers compounding together: more chips deployed in parallel, longer training runs, and newer accelerators with higher per-chip throughput. Frontier training-compute spending is doubling roughly every 8 months; power draw per frontier run is doubling annually. For context, the doubling time across all machine-learning history before 2010 was much slower (~20 months in the original 2018 OpenAI analysis). The post-2010 acceleration is the empirical anchor for the "4th industrial revolution as compute revolution" framing.

raw_evidence.label: Moore's Law slowdown — the compute side of the 4th-revolution story
raw_evidence.content: Moore's Law — Gordon Moore's 1965 observation that transistor counts per integrated circuit roughly double every two years — drove the third industrial revolution and underwrote the fourth. The OWID transistors-per-chip series in this bundle (1971-2021, 39 data points, Intel 4004 → modern multi-core CPUs) traces the long arc. But the cadence has slowed: Intel's then-CEO Brian Krzanich publicly conceded in 2015 that the cadence had moved "closer to two and a half years than two," and industry observers describe the post-2010 transistor-density growth as linear rather than exponential. Continued advances now come from EUV lithography, gate-all-around transistors, and 2nm-class processes (Intel 18A, TSMC N2, Samsung 2nm), but each new node costs far more and adds less. The interpretive hook for the AI-compute story is sharp: at the moment AI training compute started doubling every six months (2010 onwards), the per-chip transistor density underneath it started growing more slowly. The compute curve is steeper than ever, but the chips are no longer carrying it — the multiplier is now parallelism, runtime, and raw electricity.

raw_evidence.label: Data centres are the new heavy electricity consumer
raw_evidence.content: The IEA's 2025 Energy and AI report quantifies what the spike at the right edge of the AI-compute curve means for the grid. Global data-centre electricity consumption was about 415 TWh in 2024 — roughly 1.5% of world electricity. The Base Case forecast has it growing ~15% per year (more than 4x the growth rate of all other sectors combined) to ~945 TWh by 2030, by which point data centres would draw just under 3% of world electricity. AI is the primary driver: electricity use by accelerated servers — the GPU-and-TPU racks that dominate AI workloads — is projected to grow ~30% per year. A frontier training run already consumes gigawatt-hours of electricity over weeks or months on thousands of high-end accelerators. Most regional grids are not built for this profile: hyperscale campuses now routinely request 100 MW+ interconnections, with some planned to gigawatt scale, but the transmission upgrades required to deliver that power take 5-10 years to plan, permit, and build.

raw_evidence.label: Training power draw — frontier runs now 100+ MW, doubling annually
raw_evidence.content: Where power-draw is recorded (214 models out of 1018), training-run electricity demand has scaled from a few kilowatts in the mid-2010s to over 100 MW in 2025. Max training power by year: 2015 = 2.1 kW (small academic experiments); 2018 = 209 kW (BERT-era); 2020 = 5.1 MW (GPT-3 scale); 2022 = 4.2 MW; 2023 = 38.4 MW; 2025 = 109.9 MW (Grok 3). That is roughly an order of magnitude per 4 years, or doubling annually — consistent with Epoch AI's separate published finding on frontier training-run power. 100 MW for a single training run, sustained for weeks or months, is in the same league as a steel mill or a mid-sized data centre, but concentrated on one workload. The grid implication is straightforward: hyperscalers now plan for gigawatt-scale campuses, because they expect the next-gen frontier runs to use that capacity.
raw_evidence.code:
pw = ai.dropna(subset=["pub_year", "Training power draw (W)"])

pw_by_year = pw.groupby(pw.pub_year.astype(int))["Training power draw (W)"].agg(["count", "median", "max"]).reset_index()
pw_by_year.columns = ["Year", "n_models", "median_W", "max_W"]
print(pw_by_year.tail(15).to_string(index=False))
# Compute median power draw for frontier (top-decile by compute) per year, post-2015
print("\nMax training power by year, post-2015:")
for y in range(2015, 2027):

    if not r.empty:
        print(f"  {y}: {r.max_W.iloc[0]:.2e} W  (n={int(r.n_models.iloc[0])})")

raw_evidence.label: Data centres are the new heavy electricity consumer
raw_evidence.content: The IEA's 2025 Energy and AI report quantifies what the spike at the right edge of the AI-compute curve means for the grid. Global data-centre electricity consumption was about 415 TWh in 2024 — roughly 1.5% of world electricity. The Base Case forecast has it growing ~15% per year (more than 4x the growth rate of all other sectors combined) to ~945 TWh by 2030, by which point data centres would draw just under 3% of world electricity. AI is the primary driver: electricity use by accelerated servers — the GPU-and-TPU racks that dominate AI workloads — is projected to grow ~30% per year. A frontier training run already consumes gigawatt-hours of electricity over weeks or months on thousands of high-end accelerators. Most regional grids are not built for this profile: hyperscale campuses now routinely request 100 MW+ interconnections, with some planned to gigawatt scale, but the transmission upgrades required to deliver that power take 5-10 years to plan, permit, and build.

sentences.summary: det_05: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years. Source: Vaclav Smil interview — Fundación Naturgy (https://www.fundacionnaturgy.org/en/vaclav-smil-replacing-fossil-fuels-with-rene) Facts: Smil: replacing fossil fuels with renewable energies is a task that will inevitably occupy us for several generations. Source: Energy Transitions — Penn State GEOG/EME 432 (summarising Smil) (https://www.e-education.psu.edu/geog432/node/450) Facts: Past shifts to new primary energy sources took decades from the beginning of production to become more than insignificant contributors.; Then another two to three decades before capturing a quarter or a third of their respective energy markets.

raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.

raw_evidence.label: Vaclav Smil: energy transitions take decades, not years
raw_evidence.content: Energy historian Vaclav Smil has spent his career documenting that primary-energy transitions are slow. He defines an energy transition as the time between a new primary source being introduced and its rise to a substantial share of the market — and notes that historically every such transition took decades from first production to even modest market share, and another 2-3 decades to capture a quarter or a third of the market. The wood-to-coal-to-oil-to-gas trajectory took more than a century; he argues the renewables transition will occupy generations rather than years. This is the most important interpretive frame for the stacked-area energy chart: each fuel didn't "replace" its predecessor cleanly, it stacked on top. World coal consumption is higher now than at any point in the steam era; oil consumption is higher now than during the post-war boom. Each revolution added a new fuel rather than substituting for the old one — which is why CO2 only ever cumulatively rises.
